explanation.text: The June 2022 HTTP standard (RFC 9110, RFC 9111, RFC 9112) is the worldwide standard, and RFC 9112 confirms the authority-form of request-target applies only to CONNECT requests. No evidence in the supplied sources states that a DELETE request establishes a tunnel per this standard.
CONNECT method (RFC 7231 §4.3.6) is the HTTP method that requests establishing a tunnel, as documented in the same RFC lineage. DELETE is a state-changing method unrelated to tunnel establishment.
Tunnel behavior is defined as a blind relay between connections (RFC 9110 §3.7), but no cited source associates initiating a tunnel with a DELETE request under the June 2022 HTTP standard.

All such methods ought to be registered within the "Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Method Registry" maintained by IANA, as defined in Section 8.1. The set of methods allowed by a target resource can be listed in an Allow header field (Section 7.4.1). However, the set of allowed methods can change dynamically. When a request method is received that is unrecognized or not implemented by an origin server, the origin server SHOULD respond with the 501 (Not Implemented) status code. excerpts.text: The HTTP DELETE method is a request verb used to ask a server to remove the resource identified by a URL. In REST-style APIs it usually targets a specific object, such as a file, record, or account, and the server decides whether the caller has permission to delete it.

The DELETE method is one of the core HTTP verbs, and its security significance comes from the fact that it maps a network request to a destructive action on a specific server-side object. In practice, a DELETE endpoint should be designed so that only the intended resource can be removed, and only by callers that are authorised to perform that operation.

Because DELETE changes state, it should be treated as a privileged operation rather than a mere transport detail. API design choices such as path structure, object identifiers, and method handling determine whether the request deletes the correct object or becomes a path to accidental or malicious removal.
